Dürrenmatt was also a **painter** and draughtsman.

abschnitte.text: Friedrich Dürrenmatt was born in **1921** in Konolfingen in the **Emmental**; his father was a pastor. He studied in Bern and Zurich and at first wanted to become a painter. Then he decided to write. From the 1950s he lived in **Neuchâtel**, where he died in **1990**. Today the **Centre Dürrenmatt** there shows his paintings and drawings.

In this play the rich **Claire Zachanassian** returns to her poor home town of **Güllen**. She offers the town a billion if someone kills **Alfred Ill**. He had betrayed her when she was young. At first everyone is outraged, but slowly the townspeople give in to temptation. The play asks how much justice and morals are worth when money is involved.

In the comedy **“The Physicists”** from 1962, three physicists live in the sanatorium “Les Cerisiers” and pretend to be mad. The physicist **Möbius** wants to protect the world from his dangerous discoveries this way. But the plan fails. In his **“21 Points on The Physicists”**, Dürrenmatt wrote that a story has only been thought through to the end when it has taken the **worst possible turn**. In the play, this turn happens by chance.

Dürrenmatt also wrote exciting crime novels. In **“The Judge and His Hangman”**, the sick Inspector **Hans Bärlach** investigates in Bern and on Lake Biel. He uses the culprit as a tool to bring an old enemy to justice. “The Pledge” is another well-known crime novel of his. Many of his books are read in schools and have been made into films.

gewusst: Dürrenmatt called many of his plays comedies, even though they ask very serious questions.
The Centre Dürrenmatt in Neuchâtel was built by the Ticino architect Mario Botta.

teile.einleitung: A **foreign word** is a word that has been taken from another language and still seems foreign. You can often recognise it by its spelling or pronunciation, as with the German words “Chauffeur” (driver) or “Rhythmus” (rhythm).
wichtigste: A **foreign word** still gives away its origin through its spelling or pronunciation.
If a word has fully adapted, it is called a **loanword**, for example the German “Fenster” (window).
Many foreign words in German come from **Latin**, **Greek**, **French** and **English**.
Latin words ending in “-um” often form their German plural with “-en”: Museen (museums), Daten (dates).
In Switzerland many words from French are common, such as “Trottoir” (pavement).

abschnitte.text: Languages are constantly borrowing words from each other. A **foreign word** still seems foreign: in German, “Chauffeur” is spelt the French way and “Computer” the English way. A **loanword**, on the other hand, has fully adapted. “Fenster” comes from the Latin “fenestra”, but today it sounds completely German. Often the line between the two is blurred.

Many foreign words from science and education come from **Greek** or **Latin**. The German “Bibliothek” means a collection of books and is written with “th”. “Atmosphäre” (atmosphere) comes from “atmos” (vapour) and “sphaira” (ball). “Rhythmus” contains the letter h twice, and the y is pronounced like the German ü. Latin words ending in “-um” have special plural forms: “Museum” becomes “Museen” and “Datum” becomes “Daten”.

In Switzerland a particularly large number of words from **French** are in use. People say “Trottoir” for the pavement, “Velo” for the bicycle, “Perron” for the railway platform and “Glace” for ice cream. “Trottoir” comes from the French verb “trotter”. “Ingenieur” (engineer) also keeps the French spelling with “-ieur” and is pronounced roughly “Inschenjör”.

Today many new German words come from **English**, especially from technology, sport and music. They are called **anglicisms**, for example “Computer”, “Team” or “Download”. Some words only sound English but are not actually used that way in English. The best-known example is **“Handy”**: in English you say “mobile phone”.

gewusst: “Handy” is a false anglicism: the word looks English, but in English it is not used for a mobile phone.
Many Swiss expressions such as “Velo” or “Billett” (ticket) are not immediately understood in Germany.

teile.einleitung: The Halbtax, or Half Fare travelcard, is a pass for public transport in Switzerland. Anyone who has one pays only about half the price for most tickets.
wichtigste: With the Half Fare travelcard most tickets cost about half price.
It is valid on trains, buses, trams, many boats and mountain railways.
The Half Fare travelcard is personal and valid for one person only.
You buy it for a certain period, usually a year.
It is worth it for anyone who travels on public transport fairly often.
Today the Half Fare travelcard is stored on the **SwissPass**.

abschnitte.titel: What the Half Fare travelcard is
abschnitte.text: The word **Halbtax** means “half fare”, that is half price. With this pass you buy a ticket but only pay about half the normal price. This applies to single tickets, day passes and many other offers. The Half Fare travelcard has existed in Switzerland for many decades, and a great many people own one.

The Half Fare travelcard is not only valid with **SBB**. Many other railways, PostBuses, town buses, trams and boats also give the reduction. You also get a discount on many **mountain railways**. Some railways or special offers have their own rules, so it is worth checking the railway’s information.

The Half Fare travelcard belongs to exactly one person. You may not lend it to anyone. Today it is stored on the **SwissPass**, a red card with a photo. When tickets are checked, you show the card or your phone with the app. Anyone travelling at half price without a valid pass has to pay a surcharge.

The Half Fare travelcard itself costs money. It is worth it if you travel so much in a year that the saving is bigger than the price of the pass. Anyone who travels almost every day often chooses the **General Abonnement**, **GA** for short. With it you can travel all over Switzerland without individual tickets.

gewusst: The Half Fare travelcard is one of the most popular passes in Switzerland; a large part of the population owns one.
Since 2015 the Half Fare travelcard and the GA have been stored on the SwissPass; before that there were separate cards for them.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who rents a flat draws up a **handover report** when moving in and when moving out. It records the condition of the flat and what was already broken. This protects you later from arguments and unnecessary costs.
wichtigste: The handover report describes the condition of the flat.
The tenant and the landlord go through the flat together.
Existing defects are written down precisely, ideally with photos.
Both sign, and both get a copy.
Whatever is in the report was already broken before.
This means you do not have to pay for someone else’s damage when you move out.

abschnitte.text: A **handover report** is a document that is filled in when a rented flat is handed over. Room by room, you record what the walls, floors, windows, kitchen and bathroom look like. The number of **keys** and the meter readings are also noted. In Switzerland this is often also called the **flat inspection**.

When moving in you look carefully: scratches in the parquet, marks on the wall, a crack in the washbasin. Every such **defect** goes into the report. Dated photos help as well. If you only notice something later, you report it to the landlord quickly and **in writing**.

When moving out, the flat is inspected together again. The condition is compared with the report from moving in. The tenant does not have to pay for damage that was already there before. Normal **wear and tear**, such as walls that have faded slightly after many years, is part of living somewhere and is not at the tenant’s expense.

Many landlords ask for a **rent deposit**. In Switzerland it may be at most three months’ rent and is kept in an account in the tenant’s name. After moving out you get the money back if there is no new damage. So a careful report also helps you get your deposit back in full.

gewusst: You should only sign a report if you agree with what it says.
If there is an argument later, the signed report is an important piece of evidence.

teile.einleitung: Service charges are costs of a rented flat that come on top of the actual rent, for example for heating, hot water or the caretaker. Swiss tenancy law has an important rule about them.
wichtigste: Service charges pay for services around the flat, such as heating and hot water.
The landlord may only charge them if they are **listed individually** in the tenancy agreement.
If they are not in the contract, they are considered **included in the rent**.
Often you pay a monthly **payment on account**.
Once a year a **statement** arrives with the actual costs.
Tenants may see the receipts.

abschnitte.text: The **rent** pays for the use of the flat itself. In addition there are costs for things you need all the time: **heating**, **hot water**, cleaning the stairwell, the **caretaker**, the lift or charges for water and sewage. These are called **service charges**. Electricity in your own flat is usually paid directly to the electricity company.

The **Code of Obligations** says: the landlord may only charge service charges if they are expressly agreed in the **tenancy agreement**. Each item must be named **individually**, for example “heating” or “caretaker”. If the contract says nothing at all about them, the service charges are considered **included** in the rent. The landlord cannot then charge them on top.

Often you pay a fixed amount for the service charges every month along with the rent. With a **payment on account**, this is an advance payment. Once a year the landlord draws up a **statement** with the real costs. If you have paid too much, you get money back; otherwise you have to pay the difference. With a **flat rate**, the amount stays fixed and there is no statement.

Tenants have the right to see the **receipts** for the service charge statement. This lets you check whether everything is correct. If the statement shows a large extra payment, it is worth taking a close look. Advice centres such as the tenants’ association or the **conciliation authority** can help with questions.

gewusst: In many flats heating costs are the largest part of the service charges.
Anyone who heats economically and does not shower for too long can lower their own service charges when there is a statement on account.

teile.einleitung: A payment on account (Akontozahlung) is an advance payment towards costs that you will only know exactly later. At the end there is a final statement, and you either pay a bit more or get money back.
wichtigste: Akonto means advance payment or payment on account.
The word comes from Italian and means “on account”.
If you rent a flat, you often pay the service charges on account every month.
Once a year the service charge statement arrives with the real costs.
If you have paid too little, you pay the difference; otherwise you get a refund.
There are also payments on account for taxes and electricity.

abschnitte.text: The word **akonto** comes from the Italian “a conto” and means “on account”. So you pay an amount now, even though the exact costs have not been fixed yet. The amount is an **estimate**. Only later, when everything has been added up, do you know how much it really cost.

abschnitte.titel: Service charges in a rented flat
abschnitte.text: Anyone who rents a flat often pays **service charges** on top of the actual rent. These include, for example, heating, hot water, the caretaker or cleaning the stairwell. Because these costs vary depending on the winter and how much is used, you pay a fixed amount **on account** every month. Once a year the management sends the **service charge statement** with the real costs.

In the statement, the payments on account are compared with the real costs. If the winter was cold and a lot of heating was used, the money may not be enough. Then there is an **extra payment** to make. If you have paid more than necessary, you get a **refund**. It is different with a **flat rate**: this is not settled at the end of the year; you always pay the same amount.

The system is also used for **taxes**. Many cantons send provisional bills, and you pay in instalments in advance. The final bill only comes once the tax return has been checked. It is similar with some electricity or gas bills. Anyone making payments on account should put some money aside for the final statement.

gewusst: You may look at the service charge statement carefully: tenants have the right to see the receipts for it.
If the payments on account are set too low, a large extra payment may come at the end of the year.

teile.einleitung: Motor vehicle liability insurance is insurance that every car, motorbike and other motor vehicle in Switzerland must have. It pays for damage that you cause to other people with the vehicle.
wichtigste: Motor vehicle liability insurance is **compulsory** in Switzerland.
Without it you do not get **number plates**.
It pays for damage you cause to **others**.
It does not cover damage to your own car.
For that there is voluntary **comprehensive insurance** (Kasko).
The obligation is set out in the federal **Road Traffic Act**.

abschnitte.text: Being **liable** means that you have to take responsibility for damage and pay for it. Anyone who causes an accident with a car can do great damage to other people: to their vehicle, to their house or to their health. Such costs can be very high. **Motor vehicle liability insurance** covers these costs so that the people harmed are sure to get their money.

The federal **Road Traffic Act** requires every motor vehicle to have liability insurance. The road traffic office only issues the **number plates** if there is **proof of insurance**. If the insurance ends, the insurer reports this to the office and the plates must be handed in.

abschnitte.titel: What it pays and what it does not
abschnitte.text: Liability insurance pays for damage to **others**: to the other party’s car, to fences or street lamps, and the costs when people are injured. It does not pay for damage to **your own car**. For that there is voluntary **partial cover**, for example for hail or theft, and **fully comprehensive cover**, which also covers damage you cause to your own car.

You pay a yearly **premium** for the insurance. How much it is depends, for example, on the car, your age and previous accidents. Anyone who causes a lot of damage often has to pay more. Young new drivers usually pay more, because statistically they have accidents more often.

abschnitte.titel: When the person responsible is missing
abschnitte.text: Sometimes someone drives off after an accident, or a vehicle is not insured at all. For such cases Switzerland has the **National Guarantee Fund**. It makes sure that injured people still receive compensation. This means nobody is left without protection if they are involved in an accident through no fault of their own.

gewusst: Mofas also need liability insurance; this is shown by the yearly vignette on their number plate.
Liability insurance also pays if someone else drives your car with your permission and causes an accident.

teile.einleitung: A registered letter is a letter whose delivery the post office records precisely. The recipient has to confirm with their signature that they have received the letter.
wichtigste: With registered post the recipient confirms receipt with their signature.
If nobody is at home, the post office puts a collection notice in the letterbox.
The post office keeps registered items for 7 days.
For letters from authorities, a letter is often deemed to have been delivered on the last day of this period.
With a tracking number you can follow where the letter is at the moment.
Important letters such as notices of termination are often sent by registered post.

abschnitte.text: A **registered letter** is a letter sent with **proof**. The post office registers the letter when it is handed in and records when and to whom it was handed over. The recipient confirms with their **signature** that they have received it. This means the sender can later prove that the letter arrived. Registered post costs more than an ordinary letter.

If nobody is at home when the letter is delivered, the postman or postwoman puts a **collection notice** in the letterbox. It says where you can collect the letter, usually at a post office. The post office keeps the item for **7 days**. If you do not collect it, it goes back to the sender. You can also send another person with a **written authorisation** to collect it.

For letters from **authorities** or courts there is an important rule. Anyone who has to expect such a letter, for example because proceedings are under way, cannot avoid it. If they do not collect the registered letter, it is still deemed to have been delivered on the **last day of the period**. This is called **deemed delivery**. Time limits for replying then start to run anyway.

Letters where **proof** matters are sent by registered post. These include notices ending a tenancy, an insurance policy or a job. Authorities also often send important decisions by registered post. With the **tracking number** on the receipt you can follow online where the letter is at the moment.

gewusst: With a notice of termination, what often counts is not when it was sent but when the letter reaches the recipient. That is why it is better to send it early.
Anyone going on holiday can ask the post office to hold their letters and so will not miss a collection deadline.

teile.einleitung: Mail forwarding is a post office service after you move house. The post office then forwards letters and parcels that are still sent to your old address to your new address for a certain time.
wichtigste: Mail forwarding helps after a move.
Letters to your old address go to your new address for a period you choose.
You can set up forwarding online or at the post office counter.
You should set it up a few days before you move.
You still tell all important offices your new address.
You also report your move to the **municipality**.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who moves often still gets post at their old address at first. With **mail forwarding** you let the **post office** know. It then forwards letters and often parcels too to the new address for a period you choose. This means no important bill or invitation gets lost. You can set up forwarding for one person or for the whole household.

You can set up mail forwarding with Swiss Post **online** or at the **counter** of a post office. You give the old and the new address and choose from when and for how long post should be forwarded. It is best to do this a few days before the move. Depending on how long it lasts, the service costs something.

Mail forwarding only lasts for a certain time. That is why you still tell everyone your **new address**: family and friends, your school or employer, the bank, the **health insurance fund** and insurance companies. You also have to change magazine subscriptions. This way, after the forwarding ends, post comes straight to the right address.

In Switzerland you must also report a move to the **municipality**. You deregister with the old municipality and register with the new one, usually at the **residents’ registration office**. There is a short time limit for this. In many cantons this can now be done online with the **eUmzugCH** service. If you move within the same municipality, you only report the new address.

gewusst: If you ask, the post office can also hold your post, for example during a long holiday, and deliver it all at once later.
Letters that cannot be delivered are sent back by the post office to the sender, if the sender’s address is on the envelope.

teile.einleitung: An identity card or a passport shows who you are. If you lose an identity document, you must report the loss to the police and order a new one.
wichtigste: You report a lost identity document to the police.
The document is then entered in the search system and blocked.
A document reported as lost is invalid, even if you find it again.
You apply for a new document at the responsible office in the canton.
Anyone who loses their document abroad contacts the police and the Swiss embassy or consulate.
A copy of your document at home can help.

abschnitte.text: With an **identity card** or a **passport** you can prove who you are. You need them for travelling abroad, for some dealings with the authorities or when opening a bank account. An identity document contains your name, date of birth, photo and other information. That is why it is valuable and should be kept safe.

If the document has gone, you report the loss to the **police**. They enter it in the **search system**. This blocks it so that no one else can use it. If you find the document later, it is still **invalid**. You may not use it any more. The police issue a confirmation that the loss has been reported.

Then you order a new document. In most cantons you make an appointment at the **passport office** for this. A new photo is taken there, and you give your fingerprints if you are ordering a passport. For children, the parents must give their consent. The new document arrives by post after a few days. It costs money, and the price depends on the type of document.

If the document is lost on a journey, you report it to the local police. Then you contact the **Swiss embassy** or a consulate. There you get help to travel home, for example a provisional travel document. A **copy** or a photo of the document makes the process much easier.

gewusst: An identity card for children and young people under 18 is valid for five years, and for adults for ten years.
For some years now the Swiss passport has contained a chip with the person’s data.

teile.einleitung: Many German words are made up of two words. Often there is a small sound between the two parts that joins them, like the “s” in “Arbeitsplatz” (workplace). This joining piece is called a linking element.
wichtigste: A word made of other words is called a compound.
The linking element sits where two parts of the word meet.
Common linking elements are s, es, n, en, er and e.
A linking element is not a case ending like the genitive.
Many compounds manage without a linking element at all, for example “Haustür” (front door).
Switzerland has some linking elements of its own, as in “Zugsverspätung” (train delay).

abschnitte.text: In German you can join words together like building blocks. This creates **compounds**, for example “Haustür” (front door), “Schulweg” (way to school) or “Arbeitsplatz” (workplace). The last part is called the **base word**; it decides the word class and the gender. The first part is called the **modifier**; it says more precisely what is meant. So an “Arbeitsplatz” is a place where you work.

The **joint** is the seam between the two parts. Sometimes there is an extra sound there, the **linking element**. Examples are “Arbeit**s**platz” (workplace), “Sonne**n**schein” (sunshine), “Kind**er**garten” (nursery school), “Tag**es**licht” (daylight) and “Hund**e**hütte” (dog kennel). If there is nothing in between, as in “Haustür”, it is called a **zero link**.

The “s” in “Arbeitsplatz” looks like a genitive ending, but it is not one. “Arbeit” (work) is feminine and forms its genitive without an “s”: “der Arbeit”. So the linking element has no grammatical meaning in the sentence. It often makes the word easier to pronounce. Which link a word gets does not follow a simple rule; people usually just learn it along the way.

In Swiss Standard German there are some links that are different in Germany. In Switzerland people say “Zugsverspätung” (train delay) or “Zugsabfahrt” (train departure), while in Germany it is usually “Zugverspätung”. “Schweinsbraten” (roast pork) with a linking s is also usual in Switzerland and Austria. Differences like these are among the **Helvetisms**. Both forms are correct in their own country.

gewusst: Sometimes a letter even disappears when words are put together: “Schule” (school) and “Buch” (book) become “Schulbuch” (school book).
A word such as “Bundesrat” (Federal Council) contains the linking element “es”.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who moves to another municipality must deregister with the old municipality and register with the new one. This way the authorities always know where someone lives.
wichtigste: You deregister at the residents’ registration office of your previous municipality.
In the new municipality you register within a time limit.
The canton sets the time limit for registering; it is often 14 days.
In many municipalities you can also report a move online.
Swiss citizens usually need their certificate of origin to register.
The post office, health insurance fund and other offices should also be told the new address.

abschnitte.text: Every municipality in Switzerland keeps a **register of residents**. It shows who lives in the municipality. The **residents’ registration office** is responsible for it; sometimes it is called residents’ services. The municipality needs this information, for example, for taxes, for school and for the right to vote. That is why it needs to know when someone leaves or arrives.

Anyone moving away deregisters with the **old municipality**. You say when you are moving out and where to. Swiss citizens get back their **certificate of origin** if it was deposited with the municipality. The certificate of origin shows in which municipality you have your place of citizenship. Deregistering is also important when moving abroad.

At your new place of residence you register **within the time limit** set by the canton. This is often 14 days after moving in. You bring an identity document, your certificate of origin or, for foreign nationals, the residence permit, and sometimes the tenancy agreement. In many municipalities you can conveniently deregister and register online with the **eUmzugCH** service.

Once you have dealt with the municipality, not everything is done yet. The **post office** can forward letters to your new address. The health insurance fund, bank, employer and school also need the new address. Anyone who has a dog or owns a car must re-register these too. A list helps you not to forget anything.

gewusst: For taxes in Switzerland, what usually counts is where you live at the end of the year: if you move in December, you pay tax for the whole year in the new place.
There are more than 2000 municipalities in Switzerland, and each keeps its own register of residents.

teile.einleitung: In online shopping you pay over the internet for goods, services or things in games and apps. Even if you only tap a button, it costs real money.
wichtigste: Purchases in games and apps also cost **real money**.
Children ask their **parents** first before every purchase.
Such purchases in apps are called **in-app purchases**.
Parents can block purchases on devices or require a password.
In Switzerland there is no general right to cancel online purchases.
Watch out for fake online shops.

abschnitte.text: You can buy almost anything on the internet: clothes, books, games, music or holidays. You choose something, put it in the **basket** and pay, for example with a card or a payment app. It is convenient because you do not have to go to a shop. But precisely because it is so easy, you can quickly spend more money than you planned.

Many games on a tablet or mobile phone are free at first. Later, though, they offer coins, gems, characters or new levels for money. These are called **in-app purchases**. The colourful game currencies do not look like money, but they cost **real francs**. That is why you always ask your **parents** first before you buy anything.

Children and young people under 18 are usually only allowed to make bigger purchases **with their parents’ consent**. Parents can set mobile phones and tablets so that every purchase needs a **password** or is blocked completely. It helps to agree together how much money you may spend on games, for example from your own **pocket money**.

Unlike in the European Union, in Switzerland there is **no general right of withdrawal** for online purchases. Whether you can return something depends on the shop’s **terms and conditions**. That is why you read what the seller says about it before buying. Many shops offer returns voluntarily.

There are **fake online shops** that take your money and deliver nothing. Warning signs are extremely low prices, no address for the seller and payment in advance only. Emails or messages asking for passwords or card details are also often fraud. This is called **phishing**. If in doubt, ask an adult.

gewusst: Some games are designed so that you keep spending small amounts, which add up to a lot of money.
Experts advise always converting game currencies into francs in your head so that you see the real price.

teile.einleitung: “Grüezi” is the best-known greeting in German-speaking Switzerland. With this little word you show other people that you notice them and that you are being friendly to them.
wichtigste: “Grüezi” is a greeting from German-speaking Switzerland.
You say it mainly to people you address formally with “Sie”.
If you greet several people, you say “Grüezi mitenand”.
Among friends and in the family people tend to say “Hoi” or “Sali”.
In western Switzerland people greet each other with “Bonjour”, and in Ticino with “Buongiorno”.
A greeting in the stairwell makes living together friendlier.

abschnitte.text: The word “Grüezi” is a short form. In the past people said “Gott grüez i”, which means roughly “God greet you”. Over time the greeting got shorter and shorter. Today hardly anyone thinks of the old meaning. It is similar with the southern German “Grüss Gott”.

In Switzerland it depends on whom you are greeting. You say **Grüezi** to adults you do not know well, that is to people you address formally with **“Sie”**. To friends and children people tend to say **Hoi**, **Sali** or **Salü**. In Bern you often hear **Grüessech**. When saying goodbye, people say for example “Uf Widerluege” (goodbye) or “Tschüss” (bye).

Switzerland has four national languages. In **western Switzerland** people greet each other with “Bonjour”, in **Ticino** with “Buongiorno” or “Ciao”. In Romansh people say **“Allegra”**. Anyone travelling in another part of the country will please people if they greet them in their language.

A greeting is a sign of **respect**. Anyone who greets the neighbours in the stairwell is showing: I see you, we live here together. That way you get to know each other over time and are more likely to help each other. On hikes in the mountains, even people who do not know each other at all often greet each other. A friendly look goes with it.

gewusst: Abroad, “Grüezi” is seen as typically Swiss and often appears on postcards and souvenirs.
In Romansh the greeting is “Allegra”, which means something like “Be glad”.

teile.einleitung: How long does a story last? Here we distinguish between two times: the **discourse time**, which is how long it takes to read, and the **story time**, which is how long the plot lasts.
wichtigste: The **discourse time** is the time you need to read or tell the story.
The **story time** is the period of time the plot covers.
You can read a book about many years in just a few hours.
Skipping time **compresses** it; describing it in detail **stretches** it.
With **flashbacks** a story jumps into the past.

abschnitte.text: The **discourse time** is measured in pages or in reading time. The **story time** is how long the plot lasts within the story. A novel can describe a character’s whole life over 80 years, but you read it in a few hours. The other way round, a single minute can be described over many pages.

If the discourse time is shorter than the story time, this is called **time compression**: “Three years passed.” If both last about the same, the telling **matches** the time, for example in a conversation in direct speech. If the discourse time is longer, it is called **time stretching**. This happens when an exciting moment is described with lots of thoughts and details.

Not every story is told in order. In a **flashback** you find out what happened earlier. A **flash-forward** gives away what will happen later. Jumps like these make a story exciting and help you understand the characters better.

gewusst: The novel “Ulysses” by James Joyce tells of a single day in 1904 over many hundreds of pages.
A short sentence such as “Many years later” can skip decades in a story.

teile.einleitung: A smoke alarm is a small device on the ceiling that detects smoke. As soon as smoke gets into it, it beeps very loudly. This means people are warned of a fire in time, even when they are asleep.
wichtigste: When you are asleep you cannot smell smoke.
The smoke alarm gives a very loud warning sound when there is smoke.
In a fire, the poisonous smoke is usually more dangerous than the flames.
Smoke alarms belong on the ceiling, ideally in the middle of the room.
You should test the alarm regularly and change the battery.
In Switzerland the emergency number for fire is 118.

abschnitte.text: A fire produces a lot of **smoke** with poisonous gases. Just a few breaths can make you unconscious. Many people who die in fires are overcome not by the fire but by the **smoke**. When you are asleep you notice nothing, because your **nose** does not warn you then.

Inside the smoke alarm there is a small **measuring chamber** with light. If smoke gets in, the light is scattered and the alarm goes **off**. Because smoke rises, it is fitted on the **ceiling**. Bedrooms, children’s rooms and the hall are especially important.

Most smoke alarms have a **test button**. If you press it, the device beeps. This is how you check whether it still works. If the alarm beeps quietly and regularly, the **battery** is usually almost flat. After about ten years you should replace the whole device.

If you hear the alarm, you leave the flat immediately and close the **doors** behind you. If there is a lot of smoke, you move low down near the floor, because the air is better there. Never use the **lift**. Outside you call the **fire brigade** on **118**.

gewusst: In Switzerland smoke alarms in flats are not compulsory everywhere, but accident prevention experts recommend them.
In Germany smoke alarms are compulsory in all federal states.

teile.einleitung: Empty glass bottles and jars are not rubbish but a valuable raw material. Anyone who takes them to the bottle bank helps to make new glass from them.
wichtigste: Empty bottles and jam jars belong at the bottle bank.
Glass can be melted down and shaped again and again.
Waste glass is sorted by the colours clear, green and brown.
Each colour becomes glass of the same colour again.
You remove lids and corks before putting glass in.
Drinking glasses, window glass and porcelain do not belong in the bottle bank.

abschnitte.text: An empty **jam jar**, a wine bottle or a little vinegar bottle does not belong in the rubbish bag. Almost every municipality has a **bottle bank** with large containers. That is where you put the glass in. You do not have to rinse it thoroughly, but it should be empty. You take off metal lids and corks first.

The containers usually have three openings: for **clear**, **green** and **brown** glass. The colours are melted down separately. This makes glass of exactly the same colour again. Even a few coloured pieces would discolour clear glass. Glass of other colours, for example blue, usually goes in with the green glass.

Glass is made from **quartz sand**, soda and lime. Waste glass is crushed, cleaned and melted at very high temperatures. New bottles and jars are shaped from it. The special thing is that glass does not lose quality in the process. It can be recycled **as often as you like**. Because broken glass melts more easily than the raw materials, recycling also saves energy.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: Not all glass may go into the container. **Drinking glasses**, window glass, mirrors, light bulbs, ceramics and **porcelain** have a different make-up and melt differently. Even small pieces of them can ruin a whole load of new glass. These things belong in the general rubbish or in the collection for building rubble, depending on the municipality. Also, you only put glass in at the permitted times, because it is noisy.

gewusst: In Switzerland a very large share of glass bottles is collected and recycled, well over nine out of ten.
Recycled glass is as good as new: a bottle can become a bottle again and again.

teile.einleitung: For many children, the way to school is the first journey they make on their own. On the way they learn to move safely in traffic. In Switzerland the saying “Warte, luege, lose, laufe” (wait, look, listen, walk) helps with this.
wichtigste: At the edge of the road you first stop and wait.
“Luege” means look, “lose” means listen.
Only when everything is clear do you cross the road.
It is best to cross the road at the zebra crossing.
Light-coloured clothes and reflective strips make children easier to see.
Many children already go to nursery school alone or with friends.

abschnitte.text: The saying comes from **Swiss German**. First you **wait** at the edge of the road. Then you **look** left and right and **listen** to hear whether a car is coming. Only when the vehicles have stopped or the road is clear do you **walk** briskly across. You should not run, or you might trip.

In Switzerland **zebra crossings** are yellow. There pedestrians have **right of way**. Even so, you wait until the cars really stop. A car needs a **braking distance** and cannot stop immediately. It helps to look the driver in the eye.

It is best for parents to practise the way to school with their child before the child goes alone. You choose the **safest** route, even if it is a bit longer. Children are smaller than adults and are hard to **see** between parked cars. That is why you cross the road where you can see well and be seen.

Many children walk to school with **friends**. The way to school is not only a route but also time to chat and discover things. The **municipality** makes sure that the way to school is reasonable. For very long or dangerous routes there is sometimes a **school bus**.

gewusst: In Switzerland many nursery school children wear a glowing triangle or a high-visibility vest so that they can be seen easily.
Children can only judge the speeds and distances of cars properly from about the age of ten.

teile.einleitung: Early New High German is a stage of the German language that is dated roughly from 1350 to 1650. During this time the language of the Middle Ages slowly changed into the German we know today.
wichtigste: Early New High German lasted roughly from 1350 to 1650.
It comes between Middle High German and New High German.
Printing helped a shared written language to spread.
Martin Luther’s translation of the Bible was read very widely and shaped the language.
In this period “min niuwes hus” became “mein neues Haus” (my new house).
The Swiss dialects have kept many old sounds, such as “Huus” for “Haus” (house).

abschnitte.text: Languages are always changing. That is why experts divide the history of German into **language stages**: Old High German, Middle High German, Early New High German and New High German. **Early New High German** forms the bridge between the language of the knights and minstrels and the German of today. The boundaries cannot be drawn precisely, so people say “roughly 1350 to 1650”.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz invented **printing** with movable type. Now books could be made much faster and more cheaply. Printers wanted as many people as possible to be able to read their books, so they adapted the spelling. The **Reformation** brought many pamphlets and sermons to the people. Martin Luther’s translation of the **Bible** into German became especially important.

Many sounds changed during this time. The long vowels i, u and ü turned into the double sounds ei, au and eu. This change is called **diphthongisation**: “zit” became “Zeit” (time) and “hus” became “Haus” (house). The other way round, some double sounds turned into simple long vowels, as with “guot”, which became “gut” (good). This second change is called **monophthongisation**.

The Swiss dialects did not take on the new double sounds. That is why in Swiss German people still say “Ziit”, “Huus” and “Lüüt” (people) today. A great deal was printed in Switzerland during this time, too. In 1531 Christoph Froschauer in Zurich published a complete German Bible, the **Zurich Bible**. Over time, the shared written language also became established in Switzerland.

gewusst: Our phrase “mein neues Haus” (my new house) would have sounded roughly like “min niuwes hus” in the Middle Ages.
The habit of writing nouns with a capital letter only spread gradually in the early modern period.

teile.einleitung: The internet connects computers all over the world. You can use it to learn, play and talk to others, but you also see things there that are frightening or not true.
wichtigste: The internet is a worldwide network of computers.
You can find knowledge, games, videos and news there.
Not everything on the internet is true or made for children.
If something frightens you, you tell an adult.
You do not give away personal details such as your address or phone number.
Children and young people can reach the Pro Juventute advice service on **147**.

abschnitte.text: The **internet** is a huge network. Millions of computers, mobile phones and other devices are connected to each other through it. The data travels through cables, by radio and even via satellites. The **World Wide Web** with its websites is only one part of it. Emails and video calls also run over the internet.

abschnitte.titel: What you can do with it
abschnitte.text: On the internet you can look up almost anything: how an animal lives, what time the train leaves or what the weather will be like. You can listen to music, watch films, play games and stay in touch with family and friends. Many schools use the internet for lessons. It is important to agree your **screen time** with your parents.

Sometimes on the internet you see pictures or videos that are shocking or make you sad. That is not your fault. It is best to close the window and tell an **adult** you trust, for example your parents or your teacher. Talking about fear helps. If you would rather talk to someone you do not know, you can call **147** in Switzerland.

Anyone can write something on the internet. That is why not everything is **true**. Some news is made up; this is called **fake news**. It helps to ask: who wrote this? Does it also appear in other, well-known places? People in chats are also not always who they claim to be.

On the internet, do not give **personal data** such as your address, school or phone number to strangers. Do not send photos to people you do not know. Never meet up alone with someone you only know from the internet. A good password protects your accounts.

gewusst: The first computers were already linked into a network in the USA around 1969, and the internet later grew out of it.
The World Wide Web was invented around 1990 at the research centre CERN near Geneva.

teile.einleitung: The **first sound shift** was a big change in pronunciation a very long time ago. Because of it, the Germanic languages, which include German and English, became different from Latin or Greek.
wichtigste: The first or **Germanic sound shift** separated Germanic from the other Indo-European languages.
It happened more than 2000 years ago; the exact date is unknown.
For example, p became f: Latin “pater”, English “father”.
K became h: Latin “centum”, German “hundert” (hundred).
**Jacob Grimm** described the rules in 1822; this is called **Grimm’s law**.
In 1875, **Karl Verner** explained apparent exceptions with stress.

abschnitte.text: Many languages of Europe and Asia are related to each other. This family is called **Indo-European**. It includes Latin, Greek, the Slavic languages and the Germanic languages. The Germanic languages, such as German, English, Dutch or Swedish, split off through a regular change in the consonants: the **first sound shift**.

Certain stop sounds turned into friction sounds: **p** became **f**, **t** became a sound like the English “th”, and **k** became **h**. You can see this by comparing words: Latin “pater” and English “father”, Latin “tres” and English “three”, Latin “centum” and German “hundert”. Other sounds shifted too, so d became t: Latin “duo”, English “two”. Latin kept the old sounds.

**Jacob Grimm**, known for the fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm, was also a language scholar. In 1822 he described the regular matches that today are called **Grimm’s law**. The Danish scholar Rasmus Rask had noticed something similar before him. Some words seemed not to follow the rules. In 1875, **Karl Verner** showed that this depended on the original **stress**. This is called **Verner’s law**.

Much later came the **second sound shift**. It separated High German from English and Dutch: English “two”, but German “zwei”. It went furthest in the south of the German-speaking area. That is why many Swiss German dialects say “Chind” instead of “Kind” (child) and “Chäs” instead of “Käse” (cheese).

gewusst: Thanks to the sound shift you can spot relatives: Latin “piscis” and German “Fisch” (fish) belong together.
The V in the German word “Vater” (father) is pronounced like an f, which still shows the shift from p to f today.

teile.einleitung: A rent deposit is a sum of money that tenants pay as security when they move in. It protects the landlord in case damage or unpaid bills are left at the end.
wichtigste: The rent deposit is **security** for the landlord.
For flats it may be at most **three months’ rent**.
The money goes into a **blocked account** in the tenant’s name.
The landlord may not use the money on their own.
After moving out, the tenant gets the deposit back with interest if everything is in order.
Instead of money, you can often take out **rent deposit insurance**.

abschnitte.text: When you move in, the landlord often asks for a **rent deposit**. It is a security. If the tenant leaves damage that they have to pay for when moving out, or has not paid the rent, the landlord can draw on it. If everything is in order, the tenant gets the money back.

The Swiss **Code of Obligations** says exactly where the deposit must go: into a **savings account** or deposit at a bank, in the **tenant’s name**. This is called a **blocked account**. So the landlord may not simply take the money into their own account. The bank only releases it if both agree or if a court or authority decides.

For **flats** the deposit may be at most **three months’ rent**. The interest on the blocked account belongs to the tenant. For business premises higher amounts are also allowed. Many landlords ask for exactly the permitted three months’ rent, which can be a lot of money for young people moving out for the first time.

After the **flat is handed back**, the landlord checks whether there is any damage. If neither has any claims left, they sign the release and the tenant receives the money. If the landlord does not make a legal claim within one year of the end of the tenancy, the tenant can ask the bank to return the money.

Anyone who does not have the money all at once can often take out **rent deposit insurance**. Then you pay a premium every year, and the insurer guarantees the amount to the landlord. This is convenient, but over the years you pay money that you do not get back. If the insurer has to pay for damage, it later reclaims the money from the tenant.

gewusst: Legally, the deposit remains the tenant’s money, even though they cannot get at it during the tenancy.
The rule that the money must be held in the tenant’s name is in Article 257e of the Code of Obligations.

teile.einleitung: Cyberbullying means that someone is repeatedly insulted, humiliated or left out via the internet or a mobile phone. It hurts just as much as bullying in the playground. But there are ways to fight back.
wichtigste: Cyberbullying is bullying through chats, social networks or messages.
It can happen around the clock, and many people see it.
Screenshots are evidence and help later.
The most important thing is to show it to a trusted adult.
You can block the bullies and report them to the provider.
Anyone watching should not join in and should not forward anything.

abschnitte.text: In **cyberbullying**, a person is torn down **again and again** through digital means. This happens, for example, in a **class chat**, on social networks or through messages. People spread nasty comments, embarrassing pictures or lies, or they deliberately leave someone out of a group. A single argument is not bullying. What is typical is that it goes on for a long time and one person is left on their own.

Bullying on the internet does not stop after school. It can go on **around the clock**, even at home. Lots of people see it, and pictures or texts can be passed on quickly. Sometimes the people affected do not even know who is behind it. This frightens many people and can make them very sad.

It is important not to insult them back. It is better to take **screenshots** of the messages, because they are **evidence**. Then you show everything to a **trusted adult**, such as your parents or a teacher. They can help to make the bullying stop. You can **block** the bullies and **report** them to the provider. You can also get advice by calling **147**, the Pro Juventute helpline.

In cyberbullying, many people are often watching. Anyone reading along can make a big difference: you **do not forward anything**, you do not join in and you show the person affected that they are not alone. You can also tell an adult. That is not telling tales but **helping**. In Switzerland some actions in cyberbullying, such as threats or insults, can also be criminal offences.

gewusst: Screenshots show who wrote what and when. That is why they are so valuable when you get help.
Many schools in Switzerland have rules for class chats so that everyone treats each other with respect.

teile.einleitung: House rules set out how people in a block of flats can live well together. They say, for example, when it should be quiet, how the laundry room is used and that the stairwell must be kept clear.
wichtigste: The house rules apply to everyone who lives in the building.
They are often part of the tenancy agreement.
The stairwell is an **escape route** and must be kept clear.
They cover quiet times, the laundry room, rubbish and tidiness.
Anyone who keeps to them shows consideration for the neighbours.
If there are problems, people first talk to each other in a friendly way.

abschnitte.text: In a building with many flats, everyone shares the **stairwell**, the cellar, the laundry room and often a garden. So that there are no arguments about this, the landlord or the management writes **house rules**. They are usually handed over together with the tenancy agreement. Anyone who moves in promises to keep to these rules.

No boxes, bikes or pushchairs may stand around in the stairwell. The reason is that it is an **escape route**. In a fire everyone must be able to get out quickly and safely, even in smoke when you can hardly see anything. The **fire brigade** needs room for its hoses and to carry people. Things standing around can also catch fire themselves.

In many Swiss buildings there is a shared **laundry room**. A rota shows who may do their washing on which day. After washing you tidy up and clean the filter. There are also rules for rubbish: rubbish bags only go out on collection day, and you separate paper, glass and other materials.

The house rules often name times when the building should be quiet, for example at **night** and sometimes over lunchtime. Then you play quietly, do not play music loudly and do not run noisy machines. The municipality often has its own rules about noise too.

If you are annoyed with a neighbour, it is best to talk to them **in a friendly way** first. Many problems are quickly solved like this. If that does not help, you can contact the **management** or the landlord. Anyone who keeps breaking the house rules can, in the worst case, lose their flat.

gewusst: The shared laundry room with a washing rota is seen as typically Swiss and is rather rare abroad.
Fire brigades warn that even a single object in the stairwell can become a trip hazard in smoke.

teile.einleitung: A notice of termination ends a contract, for example a tenancy agreement for a flat. Swiss tenancy law has precise rules so that tenants are protected.
wichtigste: A flat can only be given notice **in writing**.
The landlord must use a **form** approved by the canton.
Without this form the notice is **void**, that is invalid.
For flats a notice period of three months usually applies.
Notice is given for certain dates that are set in the contract or usual in the area.
A notice can be challenged before the **conciliation authority**.

abschnitte.titel: What a notice of termination is
abschnitte.text: With a **notice of termination**, one party to a contract says: I want to end the contract. This exists for tenancy agreements, employment contracts or subscriptions. The **tenancy law** in the Swiss **Code of Obligations** contains special rules for flats. They are meant to stop anyone suddenly finding themselves out on the street.

If the **landlord** gives notice, they must use an **officially approved form**. The canton decides what this form looks like. Among other things, it says how the tenants can defend themselves. If the form is missing, the notice is **void** and does not count at all. For a family home, the notice must be sent separately to both spouses.

The **tenant** must also give notice in writing, but without a special form. A signed letter is enough. It is best to send it by **registered post** so that you can prove when it arrived. If two spouses live in the family home, both must sign.

For flats a **notice period** of three months usually applies. Notice is given for a **date** that is in the contract or usual in the area. It is important that the notice reaches the other party before the notice period begins. Anyone who wants to move out earlier can often suggest a suitable **replacement tenant**.

If you think a notice is unfair, you can challenge it before the **conciliation authority** for tenancy matters. You have **30 days** to do this after receiving the notice. The authority tries to find an agreement. Sometimes the tenancy can also be **extended** if moving out would be very hard.

gewusst: A letter giving notice is usually only deemed delivered when it could be collected, not when it was sent.
In Switzerland most people rent their homes, which is why tenancy law matters to a great many people.

teile.einleitung: A lot of personal things are stored on a mobile phone: photos, messages and contacts. A screen lock makes sure that nobody can get at them without permission.
wichtigste: A screen lock protects your data from strangers.
Without a lock, anyone who finds your phone can see your photos and messages.
You can use a code, a pattern, your fingerprint or your face.
A good code is not easy to guess, so not 1234 or your birthday.
You do not tell anyone your code except your parents.
The phone should lock itself after a short time.

abschnitte.text: A lot of private things are stored on a **mobile phone**: photos, chats, contacts and often logins for apps too. Without a **screen lock**, anyone who picks up the phone can see everything. That can happen if you leave it lying around or lose it. A lock protects your **data** and also that of your friends who have written to you.

There are several ways to lock a phone. The best known is a **number code**, the PIN. Some devices allow a **pattern** that you draw with your finger. Many phones also recognise your **fingerprint** or your **face**. Even then you also need a code in case the recognition does not work.

A code is only useful if nobody can guess it. Numbers like **1234**, 0000 or your date of birth are too easy. A code with six digits that do not follow a pattern is better. You tell **nobody** your code, not even your best friend. Only your parents may know it. Make sure nobody is looking over your shoulder when you type it in.

In the settings you can set the phone to **lock automatically** after a short time. No private messages should appear on the lock screen. Many phones have a function to **locate** them if they get lost. With it you can lock the device remotely or even wipe it. It is worth setting up this function with your parents.

gewusst: After several wrong attempts many phones lock themselves for a while, so that nobody can simply try out every code.
A six-digit number code has a million possible combinations.

teile.einleitung: In subletting, a tenant rents out their flat or a room to another person. This is allowed in Switzerland, but only with the landlord’s consent.
wichtigste: Subletting is regulated in the Code of Obligations.
The tenant needs the landlord’s consent.
The landlord may only refuse for certain reasons.
One reason is an excessively high rent for the subtenant.
The main tenant remains responsible to the landlord.
If the main tenancy ends, the sublet also ends.

abschnitte.text: In **subletting** there are three people involved: the **landlord**, the **main tenant** and the **subtenant**. The main tenant has a contract with the landlord. They then make a second contract themselves with the subtenant. You can sublet the whole flat or just a **room**, for example while you are abroad.

Anyone who wants to sublet must **ask** the landlord and tell them the terms, such as the rent and how long it will last. The landlord may only say no for certain **reasons**. For example, if the tenant will not tell them the terms. Or if the subtenant would have to pay an **excessively high** rent. The landlord may also refuse if the sublet would cause them significant disadvantages.

The **main tenant** remains responsible to the landlord. If the subtenant does not pay or breaks something, the landlord has to turn to the main tenant. That is why you should choose the subtenant carefully and make a **written contract**. It states how long the sublet lasts and what it costs.

Anyone who rents out their flat for short periods to tourists through **online platforms** is usually subletting too. This also needs the landlord’s **consent**. Some municipalities and cantons have extra rules for this. Anyone who rents out without permission even risks having their tenancy **terminated**.

gewusst: A shared flat, known in German as a WG, is often also a form of subletting.
Towards the main tenant, the subtenant has similar rights to an ordinary tenant.

teile.einleitung: **Epic** or narrative literature is literature that tells stories. It includes all texts in which someone tells a story, from a short fairy tale to a thick novel.
wichtigste: Narrative literature is one of the three genres, alongside **poetry** and **drama**.
A typical feature of narrative literature is a **narrator**.
A **novel** is a longer narrative text and belongs to narrative literature.
Other forms are the fairy tale, fable, legend, novella and short story.
The oldest works of narrative literature are long heroic poems, the **epics**.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Greek “epos”, which means “word” or “story”. In narrative literature there is always a **narrator** who tells us about characters, places and events. That makes it different from drama, where the characters speak for themselves on stage. It is different from poetry because it is usually not written in verse.

Narrative literature includes long and short texts. The **novel** is long and often has many characters and storylines. The **novella** is shorter and centres on one special event. The **short story**, **fairy tale**, **fable**, **legend** and **anecdote** are also short. What they all have in common is that a story is told.

The oldest works of narrative literature are the **epics**. These are long stories in verse about heroes and gods. Famous ones are the “Iliad” and the “Odyssey”, which are said to be by the Greek poet **Homer**. In the Middle Ages, for example, the “Song of the Nibelungs” was written in the German-speaking world.

Important narrative works were also written in Switzerland. **Johanna Spyri** wrote the novels about **Heidi**, which became world famous. **Jeremias Gotthelf** wrote about life in the Emmental. **Gottfried Keller** from Zurich wrote novels and novellas, such as “Clothes Make the Man”.

gewusst: Johanna Spyri’s Heidi books have been translated into a great many languages.
Even a fable of only a few sentences belongs to narrative literature, because it too tells a story.

teile.einleitung: Anyone cycling at night or when visibility is poor needs lights. There must be a white light at the front and a red light at the back. This lets others see that you are there and which way you are going.
wichtigste: At the front there is a white light.
At the back there is a red light.
You need lights at night, at dusk, when visibility is poor and in tunnels.
A bike also needs reflectors at the back and on the pedals.
The light must be easy to see but must not dazzle.
Without lights you risk a fine and, above all, an accident.

abschnitte.text: The **white light** at the front shows others that you are coming towards them. It also helps you to see the road. The **red light** at the back shows that you are riding in front of someone. Cars have the same colours. This way everyone knows immediately which **direction** you are going in.

Lights are compulsory from **dusk** until daybreak. They must also be switched on in rain, fog or snow and in **tunnels**. In autumn and winter it gets dark early, often already on the way home from school. That is why it is better to switch the lights on once too early than too late.

As well as lights, a bike needs **reflectors**. At the back there is a red reflector, and on the **pedals** there are orange reflectors. They light up when the light from cars falls on them. Reflectors in the **spokes** make the bike visible from the side too.

There are **fixed lights**, often powered by a dynamo, and clip-on lights with a **rechargeable battery** or ordinary batteries. Clip-on lights are allowed, but you must have them with you. Before setting off you check that they **work**. A rechargeable battery should be charged in good time.

gewusst: A bike light should be adjusted so that it points slightly forwards onto the road, so that it does not dazzle anyone.
Modern LED lights use much less electricity than old light bulbs and last longer.

teile.einleitung: Waste paper is used paper that is collected and recycled. In this way old newspapers and exercise books become new paper.
wichtigste: Newspapers, magazines, exercise books and leaflets belong in the paper collection.
New paper is made from waste paper.
Recycled paper needs less wood, water and energy.
You tie the paper into bundles with string and without plastic.
Tissues, baking paper and drinks cartons do not belong in it.
In many municipalities cardboard is collected separately.

abschnitte.text: Old **newspapers**, magazines, exercise books, leaflets, letters and books without covers go into the **paper collection**. The paper should be clean and dry. You stack it and tie it into a bundle with **string**. Sticky tape and plastic bags are not wanted, because they cause problems during processing. When collections take place is shown in the municipality’s rubbish calendar.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: Not everything that looks like paper can be recycled. **Tissues** and kitchen roll are often dirty. **Baking paper** and coated paper are hard to break down. **Drinks cartons** also do not belong in the paper collection, because they contain layers of plastic and sometimes aluminium. In many municipalities cardboard is collected separately from paper.

Paper is made of fine **fibres**, which mostly come from wood. In the paper mill, waste paper is broken down with water into a pulp. Printing ink and other materials are removed. New sheets of paper are made from the pulp. The fibres can be reused several times, but they get a little shorter each time. That is why new fibres are often mixed in too.

For **recycled paper**, fewer trees have to be cut down. It also needs less water and energy than paper made from fresh wood. Exercise books and toilet paper made from recycled paper can often be recognised by an eco-label. In many Swiss municipalities, school classes or clubs collect the waste paper and earn money for their funds.

gewusst: Paper fibres can be recycled several times before they become too short.
In Switzerland a large share of used paper and cardboard is collected and recycled.

teile.einleitung: A compost heap is a place where new soil is made from plant remains. Small creatures eat the waste and over time turn it into fertile humus.
wichtigste: Plant remains such as peel, leaves and grass cuttings belong in the compost.
Worms, fungi and tiny bacteria break down the waste.
Compost turns into dark soil rich in nutrients.
Many municipalities collect green waste with a separate collection.
Biogas can also be produced from green waste in special plants.
Plastic, glass and metal never belong in the compost.

abschnitte.text: **Plant remains** go into the compost: banana skins, apple cores, vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, leaves, grass and small twigs. Wilted flowers belong there too. Plastic, glass, metal, ash from the barbecue, cat litter and diseased plants do not belong in it. In the garden people usually leave out meat and cooked food, because they can attract rats.

Many creatures work in the compost. **Earthworms** and **compost worms** eat the waste and leave behind valuable crumbs. Woodlice, millipedes and beetles break the remains into smaller pieces. Invisibly small **bacteria** and **fungi** do most of the work. This can make it really warm inside the compost heap.

After a few months the waste has turned into dark, crumbly soil. It smells like the forest floor and is called **humus**. Gardeners mix it into flower beds and pots. In this way the plants get back the **nutrients** that were in the remains. This completes a natural cycle.

Not everyone has a garden. That is why many Swiss municipalities collect **green waste** in their own containers. Each municipality decides exactly what may go in. The green waste goes to large **composting plants** or **fermentation plants**. In fermentation plants **biogas** is produced, which can be used to generate electricity and heat or to power vehicles.

gewusst: A handful of good compost contains more tiny living things than there are people on Earth.
Inside, a compost heap can get so warm that it steams on cold days.

teile.einleitung: Anyone in Switzerland who passes their driving test first gets their driving licence only on probation. This probationary period lasts three years and is meant to guide young drivers towards driving safely.
wichtigste: After passing the test you get a probationary driving licence.
The probationary period lasts 3 years.
During this time you must attend a further training course.
New drivers have an alcohol limit of 0.1 per mille, so practically no alcohol.
If the licence is withdrawn because of an offence, the probationary period is extended.
In a second serious case the licence is cancelled.

abschnitte.text: After the practical test you receive a **probationary driving licence**. It is valid for **three years**. Only when you have got through this time without any major problems and have attended the course do you receive the **full driving licence**. The probationary period is meant to show that you can drive safely without a driving instructor.

During the probationary period you must attend a **further training course**. There you learn, for example, to recognise dangers early and to judge your own abilities well. Young drivers have accidents more often because they lack **experience**. Anyone who does not take the course in time loses their probationary licence.

Anyone who commits an offence during the probationary period and has to hand in their licence gets an **extension** of the probationary period by one year. If a second such case happens, the licence is **cancelled**. Then you must later start again from the beginning, with a learner’s licence and a new test. Before that you first need an **assessment** by experts.

The word **probationary period** also exists at work. In Switzerland, with a new job, the first month counts as the probationary period; it can be extended to up to **three months**. During this time both sides can end the contract with a short **notice period** of seven days. This lets employers and employees check whether they are a good fit.

gewusst: The probationary driving licence has existed in Switzerland since 2005.
Young new drivers are involved in accidents more often, relative to their numbers, than experienced drivers; this was one reason for introducing the probationary period.

teile.einleitung: A defibrillator, AED for short, is a device that can save lives when someone’s heart stops. It is designed so that even people without training can use it.
wichtigste: AED stands for automated external defibrillator.
It is needed when the heart has stopped (cardiac arrest).
The AED gives the heart an electric shock so that it beats properly again.
The device explains step by step with a voice what you have to do.
It only gives a shock if one is needed.
First you call 144 and start chest compressions.

abschnitte.text: In **cardiac arrest**, the heart no longer pumps blood through the body. Often the heart muscle only quivers irregularly; this is called **ventricular fibrillation**. The person collapses, does not respond and no longer breathes normally. Without help the brain gets no oxygen. That is why every minute counts.

An **AED** measures the heart rhythm through two sticky electrodes on the chest. If it detects ventricular fibrillation, it gives a short **electric shock**. This can bring the heart back into a normal rhythm. The device decides by itself whether a shock is needed. That is why you cannot use it wrongly: without ventricular fibrillation there is no shock.

First you call the ambulance service on **144**. Then you start **chest compressions**: pressing hard and fast in the middle of the chest. A second person fetches the AED. When you switch the device on, it **explains with a voice** what to do. You stick on the electrodes and follow the instructions. While the shock is given, nobody touches the person.

AEDs hang in many public places, for example at **stations**, in sports halls, schools, shopping centres and municipal buildings. You can recognise them by a **green sign** with a white heart and a lightning bolt. In Switzerland there are apps and maps that show where the nearest AED is. It is worth looking out for them on your next walk.

gewusst: In cardiac arrest, the chance of survival falls sharply with every minute without help. That is why acting quickly is so important.
In a first aid course you learn how chest compressions and the AED work. In Switzerland you need this course for your driving licence.

teile.einleitung: The **narrative perspective** describes from whose point of view a story is told. Whether an “I” is speaking or an all-knowing narrator makes a big difference to how we experience a story.
wichtigste: The **first-person narrator** is a character and tells the story using “I”.
The **authorial narrator** knows everything and comments on what happens.
With the **figural** point of view you experience everything through one character, in the third person.
The **neutral narrator** only describes what can be seen from the outside, like a camera.
The narrator is not the same as the author.
In 1955, **Franz K. Stanzel** described the typical narrative situations.

abschnitte.text: With a **first-person narrator**, the storytelling voice is itself a character in the story: “I ran to the station.” You only find out what this “I” knows and feels. A well-known example is the series “Diary of a Wimpy Kid” by Jeff Kinney, in which Greg Heffley tells the story himself. There is a difference between the **narrating I**, who looks back from a distance, and the **experiencing I**, who is right in the middle of events.

The **authorial narrator** stands above the events. He knows the thoughts of all the characters, makes comments and hints at what is to come. In the **figural** narrative situation the narrator steps back, and you experience everything through one character, but with “he” or “she”. The **neutral narrator** only reports what you could see and hear, like a camera.

In 1955 the Austrian literary scholar **Franz K. Stanzel** distinguished three typical narrative situations: **authorial**, **figural** and the **first-person** narrative situation. His model is often used in German lessons. It helps you describe texts more precisely. In many books, however, the perspective changes.

Sometimes you hear a character’s thoughts directly, without “he thought”: “I hope nobody notices.” This is called an **interior monologue**. With a **flashback** the story jumps into the past to show what happened before. It is always important to remember: the narrator is an invented voice. A grown-up author can, for example, let a child tell the story.

gewusst: The same story can feel completely different when it is told from the point of view of another character.
A first-person narrator can be wrong or keep something quiet. So you should not believe everything they say.

teile.einleitung: Companies and authorities store a lot of data about people. The right of access allows you to ask what data someone holds about you.
wichtigste: Everyone has the right to find out what personal data about them is being processed.
This is set out in the Swiss Data Protection Act.
The information is usually free of charge.
The company normally has to reply within 30 days.
It is best to make the request in writing and prove who you are.
If data is wrong, you can ask for it to be corrected.

abschnitte.text: **Personal data** means any information that belongs to a particular person. This includes name, address, date of birth and phone number, but also photos, purchases or what someone does in an app. Many companies collect such data, for example online shops, insurance companies or apps. The **Data Protection Act** sets out what they are allowed to do with it.

Under the Data Protection Act, everyone may ask a company or a federal authority to find out **what data** it holds about them. The company must also say what it uses the data for, where it comes from and how long it is kept. This **right of access** applies to everyone, including children and young people. For children, the parents usually help with the request.

It is best to write a short letter or email to the company. You ask for **information** about your own data and include proof of who you are, for example a copy of your identity card. This prevents strangers from getting other people’s data. The company usually has to reply **within 30 days**. The information is normally **free of charge**.

Once you have received the information, you can use further rights. If data is wrong, you can ask for it to be **corrected**. In certain circumstances you can also ask for it to be **deleted**. If a company does not reply, you can contact the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner or take legal action.

gewusst: Switzerland’s revised Data Protection Act came into force on 1 September 2023.
For cantonal authorities, the cantons’ data protection laws apply, and they also include a right of access.

teile.einleitung: The General Abonnement, GA for short, is a travel pass for public transport in Switzerland. Anyone with a GA can travel almost everywhere by train, bus, tram and on many boats, as often as they like.
wichtigste: GA is the abbreviation for General Abonnement.
The GA is valid on almost all trains, buses, trams and many boats in Switzerland.
You can travel with it as often as you like without buying tickets.
There is a GA for 1st class and for 2nd class.
There are cheaper versions for children, young people and senior citizens.
The GA is stored on the SwissPass.

abschnitte.text: With the **General Abonnement** you can travel on almost the whole **public transport** network of Switzerland. This includes the trains of SBB and many other railways, buses, **PostBuses**, the trams in the towns and many boats on the lakes. You no longer have to buy tickets and can simply get on. The GA is valid for a year or as a monthly pass.

Today the GA is stored on the **SwissPass**, a red card. When tickets are checked, you hold out the card and the device shows whether the GA is valid. The SwissPass is also available in an app on your mobile phone. Other offers can be stored on the same card, for example a ski pass or a Mobility car-sharing subscription.

There is a GA for **1st class** and for **2nd class**. There are also cheaper versions for children, young people, students, senior citizens and people with disabilities. Families can also buy reduced-price GAs. The prices change from time to time, so it is best to look up the current ones.

The GA is valid **almost** everywhere, but not quite. On many **mountain railways**, such as cable cars and some cogwheel railways, the GA only gives a discount. Some tourist trains and boats also need a supplement. For journeys abroad, the GA is only valid as far as the border. Even so, it is very handy for people who travel a lot.

gewusst: The first General Abonnement already existed in Switzerland in the 19th century.
Many people in Switzerland own a GA and so leave the car at home more often.

teile.einleitung: **Expressionism** was a movement in literature and art from about 1910 to 1925. The artists did not want to copy reality, but to express feelings and deep inner turmoil.
wichtigste: Literary Expressionism flourished from about **1910 to 1925**.
It was a reaction to the **big city**, technology, war and the collapse of old values.
In 1911 Jakob van Hoddis launched Expressionist poetry with the poem **“End of the World”**.
In 1914 Georg Trakl wrote the anti-war poem **“Grodek”**.
Kurt Pinthus published the collection **“Twilight of Humanity”** in 1919.
Important magazines were **“Der Sturm”** (The Storm) and **“Die Aktion”** (Action).

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “expressio”, which means expression. Shortly before the **First World War** the world was changing fast: cities grew, and machines and noise shaped everyday life. Many young poets felt threatened by this world and like strangers in it. They wanted to shake people up with strong images and fierce language.

In 1911 **“End of the World”** by **Jakob van Hoddis** was published. It begins with “From the citizen’s pointed head the hat flies off” and lines up one image of disaster after another. In “The God of the City”, **Georg Heym** showed the big city as a threatening idol. **Gottfried Benn**, a doctor by profession, published the collection “Morgue” in 1912. In 1914 **Georg Trakl** experienced the Battle of Grodek as a medic and wrote the poem “Grodek” about it.
