From 1910, **Herwarth Walden** published the magazine **“Der Sturm”** in Berlin, which supported literature and art. Alongside it, **“Die Aktion”** was especially important. In 1919 **Kurt Pinthus** brought many poems together in the collection **“Twilight of Humanity”**. The title means both decline and a new beginning. **Franz Kafka** is also often placed in this period: in “The Metamorphosis” (1915), Gregor Samsa wakes up as a monstrous insect.

Painters also worked in an Expressionist way, with strong, often unnatural colours. Well-known groups were **“Die Brücke”** (The Bridge) and **“Der Blaue Reiter”** (The Blue Rider), to which Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc belonged. The painter **Paul Klee**, born near Bern, exhibited with the Blue Rider in 1912. **Dadaism** also grew out of Expressionism in Zurich in 1916.

gewusst: Franz Marc painted blue horses because colour mattered more to him than reality.
Many young Expressionists were killed in the First World War; Georg Trakl also died in 1914.

teile.einleitung: An **Elfchen** is a short poem made of exactly eleven words. The name is German and comes from “elf”, the German word for eleven. It is very popular in schools because you can write one quickly and you do not need any rhymes.
wichtigste: An Elfchen is made of **11 words**.
The words are spread over **5 lines**.
The lines have 1, 2, 3, 4 and 1 word.
An Elfchen does **not have to rhyme**.

abschnitte.text: An Elfchen has five lines with a fixed number of words: the first line has **1 word**, the second **2**, the third **3**, the fourth **4** and the last one **1 word** again. Together that makes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 = 11. That is where the name comes from.

There is often a simple guide. The first line names a colour, a quality or a topic. The second says what or who is like that. The third tells where or how it is. The fourth line often begins with “I” and says something about yourself. The last word is an ending, a kind of conclusion.

An Elfchen about summer could look like this: “Blue” in the first line, “The lake” in the second, “It sparkles brightly” in the third, “I jump in cheering” in the fourth and “Summer” in the fifth. Count them: there are exactly eleven words. With just a few words, a little picture appears in your mind.

gewusst: Because every word counts, writing an Elfchen teaches you to choose just the right words.

teile.einleitung: The alcohol limit says how much alcohol someone may have in their blood at most when driving a vehicle. Alcohol makes you slower and less careful, which is why there are strict rules on the road.
wichtigste: Per mille means “per thousand”.
0.5 per mille means half a part of alcohol per thousand parts of blood.
For most drivers in Switzerland the limit is 0.5 per mille.
New drivers with a probationary licence and learner drivers have a limit of 0.1 per mille.
The 0.5 per mille limit also applies when cycling.
The body breaks down alcohol only slowly; coffee or sleep hardly make it faster.

abschnitte.text: **Per mille** means a thousandth, so much smaller than one per cent. The figure shows how much **alcohol is in the blood**. Even a little alcohol changes your vision, your **reaction time** and your sense of danger. You often feel safer than you actually are.

For most drivers the limit is **0.5 per mille**. From 0.8 per mille, driving counts as a serious offence and is punished severely. For **new drivers**, learner drivers, driving instructors and professional drivers the limit is **0.1 per mille**. That is practically a **ban on alcohol**, because even one glass can be too much.

The **police** can ask for a breath test at any time. Anyone with too much alcohol can expect a **fine** and often the **withdrawal of their driving licence**. For new drivers the probationary period is also extended. Anyone who causes an accident under the influence of alcohol must also expect consequences with their insurance.

The limit of **0.5 per mille** does not only apply in a car but also on a **bike** and an e-bike. Anyone who has been drinking is best off leaving the vehicle where it is. Good alternatives are **public transport**, a taxi or someone who stays sober and drives.

gewusst: The body only breaks down about 0.1 to 0.15 per mille of alcohol per hour.
On the morning after a party you can still have too much alcohol in your blood, even if you feel fine again.

teile.einleitung: The Trottoir is the Swiss word for the pavement, the path for pedestrians next to the road. It is usually a little raised and separated from the carriageway by a kerb. There pedestrians are protected from cars.
wichtigste: The word Trottoir comes from French.
In Germany people say Gehweg or Bürgersteig.
Pedestrians walk on the pavement if there is one.
Since 2021 children up to the age of 12 may cycle on the pavement if there is no cycle path.
They must show consideration for pedestrians when doing so.
Cars may only park on the pavement where it is allowed.

abschnitte.text: The **pavement** lies at the edge of the road and is meant for **pedestrians**. A **kerb** separates it from the carriageway. If there is a pavement, pedestrians must use it. If there is none, they walk at the edge of the road; outside built-up areas it is best on the left-hand side, so that they face the oncoming cars.

The word **Trottoir** comes from the French “trotter”, which means something like to trot or to walk. In Switzerland and Austria it is completely normal. In Germany people tend to say **Gehweg** or Bürgersteig instead. Words like this show how the languages in Switzerland influence each other.

Since **2021**, **children up to the age of 12** in Switzerland have been allowed to cycle on the pavement if there is no cycle path or cycle lane. But they must ride **slowly** and show consideration for pedestrians. Pedestrians always have **right of way**. Older children and adults ride on the road.

You may ride on the pavement with a **kick scooter**, skateboard or inline skates. These are called vehicle-like devices. Here too the rule is: **pedestrians first**, and you do not go too fast. Electric scooters, on the other hand, count as vehicles and belong on the cycle path or the road.

gewusst: In French the pavement is still called “trottoir” today.
Lowered kerbs help people in wheelchairs and with pushchairs to get onto the pavement.

teile.einleitung: The recovery position is an important first aid measure. It is used to put an unconscious person who is breathing normally into a position in which their airways stay clear.
wichtigste: The recovery position is for people who are unconscious but breathing normally.
In this position saliva or vomit can run out of the mouth.
This keeps the airways clear so that the person does not choke.
Afterwards you call the ambulance service on 144.
You keep checking whether the person is still breathing.
If they are not breathing, chest compressions are needed.

abschnitte.text: If someone is lying on the ground, you first check whether it is **safe** for you. Then you speak to the person loudly and touch them on the shoulder. If they do not respond, they are **unconscious**. Now you check whether they are **breathing normally**: is the chest rising and falling?

If an unconscious person is lying on their back, the **tongue** can fall back and block the throat. **Saliva** or vomit can also get into the windpipe. In the **recovery position** the mouth is the lowest point, so everything runs out. The head is tilted slightly back so that air can flow freely.

You kneel next to the person and place the arm nearest to you bent upwards. You lay the other arm across their chest, with the hand against their cheek. Then you pull up the far leg by the knee and roll the person towards you onto their **side**. Finally you tilt the **head** slightly back and open the mouth a little.

Call **144** if this has not already been done. Stay with the person, cover them and keep checking their **breathing**. If they stop breathing, you roll them onto their back again and start **chest compressions**. If there is a **defibrillator** nearby, have someone fetch it.

gewusst: Anyone in Switzerland who wants a learner’s licence must first take a first aid course.
Defibrillators often hang at stations, in sports halls and shopping centres and explain how to use them with a voice.

teile.einleitung: Anyone out on foot or by bike must be easy to see in the dark. Light-coloured clothes, reflective bands and lights help drivers to spot you early. This can prevent accidents.
wichtigste: At night a driver only sees dark clothes very late.
Light colours stand out much earlier in the headlights.
Reflectors throw back the light of cars and shine brightly.
Fluorescent colours work especially well at dusk and in fog.
At night bikes need a white light at the front and a red light at the back.
Being easy to see is especially important in winter, because it gets dark early.

abschnitte.text: At night a driver only sees what their **headlights** light up. Dark clothes blend in with the road. That is why they often only notice a person in dark clothes when it is too late to **brake**. **Rain** and fog also make it harder to see.

**Reflectors** are small surfaces that throw light back exactly where it comes from. When the light of a car hits them, they light up brightly. They come as **reflective bands** for your arm, as tags on your school bag or as strips on jackets and shoes. They work best where you move, for example on your arms and legs.

**Fluorescent colours** such as neon yellow or orange stand out especially at **dusk** and in dull weather. In complete darkness they help less; then reflectors are more important. A **high-visibility vest** combines both. That is why many children wear a vest or a reflective triangle on the way to school.

Anyone riding a bike must switch on their **lights** at night and when visibility is poor: white at the front, red at the back. In addition there are **reflectors** at the back and on the pedals. Spoke reflectors make the bike visible from the side too. A bike without lights is almost invisible at night.

gewusst: Accident prevention experts estimate that with reflectors you can be seen several times further away than with dark clothes.
Many pedestrians think drivers can see them because they themselves can see the headlights well. That is a dangerous mistake.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who causes damage on a bike has to take responsibility for it. In Switzerland such damage is usually covered by private liability insurance. The former bike vignette has no longer existed since 2012.
wichtigste: Being liable means paying for damage you have caused.
Until 2011 every bike needed a bike vignette.
Since 2012 private liability insurance has paid for damage caused with a bike.
Children are often insured through their parents’ family insurance.
Private liability insurance is not compulsory but is very common.
Fast e-bikes need a number plate with their own insurance.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who causes someone **damage** has to pay for it. This is called **liability**. If, for example, you scratch a parked car with your bike, the repair can be expensive. **Liability insurance** covers such costs so that you do not have to pay everything yourself.

In the past every bike in Switzerland needed a **bike vignette**. This was a small sticker that had to be bought new every year. It included liability insurance. Since **2012** the vignette has no longer existed, because almost all households already have **private liability insurance**.

**Private liability insurance** usually covers the whole **family** living in the same household. So children are protected by their parents’ insurance. Anyone without such insurance has to **pay for damage themselves**. Private liability insurance does not cost much and protects you from very high bills.

For **slow e-bikes** up to 25 kilometres per hour, the same applies as for bikes. **Fast e-bikes** up to 45 kilometres per hour, on the other hand, need a yellow **number plate**. This requires separate liability insurance, as for a Mofa. A helmet is also compulsory for these fast e-bikes.

gewusst: Anyone who causes damage on purpose or very recklessly may get less money from the insurer.
Liability insurance does not pay for your own bike, only for damage to other people.

teile.einleitung: Old electrical appliances such as hairdryers, toasters or mobile phones contain valuable raw materials and also harmful substances. In Switzerland you can return them free of charge so that they are recycled properly.
wichtigste: Electronic waste does not belong in the general rubbish.
Shops must take back old electrical appliances free of charge.
This applies to the kinds of appliances the shop itself sells, even if you do not buy anything new.
Recycling is already paid for in the purchase price, as an advance recycling fee.
Old appliances contain metals such as copper, gold and silver.
If possible, you take out rechargeable batteries and batteries first.

abschnitte.text: **Electronic waste** means old or broken appliances that work with electricity or batteries. These include hairdryers, kettles, games consoles, mobile phones, computers, fridges and much more. These appliances are made of many different materials. That is why they must not be thrown into the **rubbish bag**.

abschnitte.titel: Back to the shop for free
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **shops are obliged** to take back old electrical appliances **free of charge**. This applies to all appliances of the kind they sell themselves, even if you do not buy anything new. So you can take an old **hairdryer** to any shop that sells hairdryers. There are also official collection points. Large appliances are often taken away when a new one is delivered.

When you buy a new appliance, you pay a small **advance recycling fee**. It is included in the price. This money later pays for the recycling. This is organised by industry organisations such as **SENS** and **Swico**. That is why returning appliances costs nothing.

In the recycling plants the appliances are taken apart and shredded. Metals such as **copper**, iron, aluminium and small amounts of **gold** and **silver** are separated from each other. These raw materials can be used again. At the same time, **harmful substances** are disposed of safely, for example from fridges or lamps. Rechargeable batteries and batteries are removed first, because they can start fires.

gewusst: A tonne of old mobile phones contains more gold than a tonne of gold ore from a mine.
Switzerland was one of the first countries to set up a nationwide system for recycling electrical appliances.

teile.einleitung: A Billett is the ticket for the train, bus, tram or boat. In Switzerland you usually buy it before getting on.
wichtigste: Billett is the Swiss word for a ticket.
On almost all trains, trams and buses you must have your ticket before the journey.
Tickets are available from machines, at the counter or in an app.
Anyone travelling without a valid ticket pays a surcharge.
Children aged 6 and over need a ticket; under 6 they travel free with an adult.
The Half Fare travelcard and the GA make travelling cheaper.

abschnitte.text: The word **Billett** comes from French and in Switzerland means a ticket. With a ticket you may travel a certain route on **public transport**. There are single tickets, day passes and season tickets. In towns there are often zones: you buy a ticket for the zones you travel through.

In Switzerland **self-checking** usually applies: you must already have your ticket **before getting on**. Ticket inspectors check it during the journey. Anyone caught without a valid ticket has to pay a **surcharge**. Only in a few cases, for example on some buses in the countryside, can you buy a ticket from the driver.

Tickets are available from **machines** at stations and stops, at **counters** and in **apps** on your mobile phone. In an app you can often simply check in and check out at the end. Then the cheapest price is worked out automatically. It is important that your phone has enough battery, because you must be able to show the ticket when it is checked.

Children under 6 travel free with an adult. Children from 6 to 16 pay a lower price. With the **Junior Card** they even travel free with a parent. Adults save with the **Half Fare travelcard**, which halves the price of many tickets. Anyone who travels very often buys a **GA**, a General Abonnement or travelcard for the whole network.

gewusst: Season tickets such as the Half Fare travelcard and the GA are stored on the SwissPass, a red card.
The Swiss rail network is very dense, and trains, buses and boats are coordinated with each other by a common timetable.

teile.einleitung: A child ticket is a cheaper ticket for children on public transport. In Switzerland small children even travel free if an adult is with them.
wichtigste: Children under 6 travel free when accompanied.
From the age of 6 a child needs their own ticket.
From 6 to 16, children usually pay a reduced price.
From 16 you pay the normal price or use a pass.
With family cards, children travel especially cheaply with their parents or grandparents.
When tickets are checked, every child must have a valid ticket.

abschnitte.text: Small children up to their 6th birthday need **no ticket** on Swiss public transport if they are travelling with someone who is at least 12 years old. They simply travel along. When it is very busy, though, people show consideration about seats: when it is full, small children often sit on someone’s lap.

From their 6th birthday a child needs their **own ticket**. Up to their 16th birthday a reduced **child price** usually applies, which costs about as much as a ticket with the Half Fare travelcard. This applies on trains, buses, trams and many boats. From 16 you pay the adult price.

There are special offers for families. With the **Junior Card**, children aged 6 to 16 travel free when they are out with their mother or father. There is a similar card for travelling with grandparents or other companions. The cards cost something once a year and are often worth it after just a few outings.

On the train the **ticket inspectors** sometimes come round. Then everyone shows their ticket or pass. Anyone without a valid ticket has to pay a **surcharge**. That is why you buy your ticket before the journey at the machine, at the counter or in the app. Children travelling alone should keep their ticket safely with them.

gewusst: In Switzerland the age limits of 6 and 16 for child tickets are the same almost everywhere, whichever railway you take.
Many children in Switzerland travel alone by bus and train to school or training from an early age.

teile.einleitung: A fat fire starts when oil or fat in the pan gets too hot and catches fire. Then you must never pour water on it. With the right method the fire can be smothered.
wichtigste: You must never pour water on burning oil.
The water turns to steam instantly and throws burning fat around.
You smother the fire with a lid or a fire blanket.
You switch off the cooker.
You do not carry the burning pan away.
If the fire gets too big, you leave the room and call the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: Oil and fat get very hot when frying. If you leave a pan on the cooker for too long, the oil can get so hot that it **catches fire by itself**. First it starts to smoke heavily. Then flames shoot out of the pan. That is why you never leave hot oil alone on the cooker.

Water is heavier than oil and sinks straight to the bottom of the hot pan. There it **turns to steam** in an instant. A little water makes a great deal of steam. This steam carries the burning fat with it and hurls it through the kitchen as a huge **jet of flame**. This is called a **fat explosion**. It can cause serious burns and set the kitchen on fire.

A fire needs **oxygen**. If you take away its air, it goes out. That is why you put a suitable **lid** on the pan or cover it with a **fire blanket**. Then you switch off the cooker and leave the lid on for a long time until everything has cooled down. You do not carry the pan away, because you could burn yourself or spill oil. There are also special **fire extinguishers** for fat fires.

In a fat fire children immediately fetch an **adult**. If the fire spreads, you leave the kitchen, close the door and call the **fire brigade** on **118**. A **fire blanket** in the kitchen is a good precaution. It hangs within easy reach on the wall and can be pulled out of its case with one tug.

gewusst: When one litre of water turns to steam, it makes well over a thousand litres of steam.
Fire extinguishers for fat fires carry fire class F.

teile.einleitung: A ball rolling onto the road is a typical dangerous situation. Anyone who runs after it can easily forget about the cars. So the rule is: stop and get help.
wichtigste: If your ball rolls onto the road, you do not run after it.
You stay at the edge of the road and fetch an adult.
Cars cannot stop immediately; they need a stopping distance.
Drivers can easily fail to see children.
The best place to play ball is the playground or sports ground.
Before crossing, the rule is: wait, look, listen, walk.

abschnitte.text: When you are playing, you only think about the **ball**. If it rolls onto the road, you want to fetch it back quickly. At exactly that moment you forget to look out for cars. That is why such accidents keep happening. The most important rule is simple: **Stop!** A ball is never as important as you are.

A car cannot stop on the spot. First the driver has to see the danger and react. Then the car rolls on a bit further until it stops. This distance is called the **stopping distance**. The faster a car is going, the longer it is. Because children are small, they are often only seen very late between parked cars.

Stay at the **edge of the road** and fetch an **adult**. They can get the ball back safely when the road is clear. If you ever have to cross the road yourself, the Swiss rule **“warte, luege, lose, laufe”** applies: stop, look left and right, listen for engines, and only go when everything is clear.

The safest place to play is where no cars drive: in the **playground**, in the school playground or on a field. Some neighbourhoods also have **shared zones**. There cars may drive at no more than 20 km/h, and pedestrians have priority. Even there, though, the rule is: keep your eyes open.

gewusst: Some warning signs for drivers show a child with a ball, so they know that children might be playing here.
In Switzerland police road safety instructors visit many school classes to practise such rules.

teile.einleitung: In the first aid course (Nothelferkurs) you learn what to do in an accident or a medical emergency until the rescue services arrive. In Switzerland you need this course before you can apply for a learner’s licence.
wichtigste: The first aid course is a **requirement** for applying for a learner’s licence.
You learn **first aid**, especially for accidents on the road.
This includes the **recovery position** and **chest compressions**.
You practise securing an accident scene and alerting the rescue services.
The course is offered, for example, by **Samaritan associations**.
When you apply, the course certificate may not be more than six years old.

abschnitte.text: In an accident every minute often counts. Until the **ambulance** arrives, people nearby can save lives. In the **first aid course** you learn how to act correctly. In Switzerland it is compulsory before you apply for a **learner’s licence**, for example for a car or a motorbike. That is why many young people take it at about 17.

abschnitte.titel: Securing the accident scene and raising the alarm
abschnitte.text: First it is about not putting yourself and others in danger. You switch on the **hazard lights**, put on a **high-visibility vest** and set up the **warning triangle**. Then you get an overview of the situation and **alert** the rescue services on **144**. You say where the accident is, what has happened and how many people are injured.

If someone is **unconscious** but breathing, you put them in the **recovery position**. This keeps the airways clear. If a person is not breathing normally, you immediately start **chest compressions**. You press hard and fast on the middle of the chest. On the course you practise this on a dummy and also learn to use a **defibrillator**, which gives the heart an electric shock.

You also learn to stop **bleeding**, for example with a pressure bandage. It is also important to calm injured people, keep them warm and not leave them alone. A motorbike helmet is only taken off in certain cases. This knowledge also helps in everyday life, in sport or at home.

The course lasts about **ten hours** and is often held over two evenings or a weekend. It is offered, for example, by **Samaritan associations** and recognised companies. At the end you receive a **course certificate**. When you apply for a learner’s licence, it may not be more than **six years** old.

gewusst: The Samaritan associations in Switzerland have existed since the 19th century.
At many stations, schools and sports facilities there are now defibrillators that even untrained people can use, because the device gives instructions.

teile.einleitung: With a hand signal on your bike you show other road users where you want to go. This way cars, bikes and pedestrians know in good time.
wichtigste: Before turning you look back over your shoulder.
If you want to turn left, you stretch out your left arm.
If you want to turn right, you stretch out your right arm.
You give the signal in good time, that is before you turn.
To turn you need both hands on the handlebars again.
At school many children practise this for the **cycling test**.

abschnitte.text: A bike has no indicator like a car. That is why you use your **arm** to show where you want to go. This lets others brake or make room. Without a signal they do not know what you are planning, and an accident can happen.

Before every turn you do a **shoulder check**. You turn your head and look behind you to see if a car or bike is coming. While doing this you keep riding as straight as possible. Only when the road is clear or the others have seen you do you give the signal and turn.

For left you stretch your **left arm** out horizontally to the side. For right you stretch out your **right arm**. The arm stays stretched out for a few seconds so that everyone can see it. Shortly before turning you put your hand back on the handlebars, because you need both hands for steering and braking.

Turning left is especially difficult because you have to cross the road. That is why the rule is: **look, signal, move into position, look again, turn**. Moving into position means riding to the middle of the road or into the left-turn lane in good time. If it seems too dangerous to you, you may get off and push your bike across the road on foot.

In many cantons, children at primary school learn the most important rules with the **traffic police**. Afterwards they often take a cycling test on the road. There you show that you have mastered hand signals, shoulder checks and right of way. You can practise first in a quiet open space.

gewusst: In Switzerland hand signals are compulsory for cyclists when they change direction.
Horse riders also use their arm on the road to show where they want to go.

teile.einleitung: 147 is the telephone number on which children and young people in Switzerland can get help when they are worried about something. The service is run by the Pro Juventute foundation.
wichtigste: By calling 147, children and young people in Switzerland reach the Pro Juventute advice service.
The advice service can be reached around the clock, including at night and at weekends.
The call is free.
The advice is confidential: what you tell them stays with the advice service.
You can also get in touch by chat, text message or email.
In an acute emergency you call the emergency numbers, for example 144 for an ambulance.

abschnitte.text: The number **147** is an advice service for children and young people. Behind it is **Pro Juventute**, a large Swiss foundation that works for young people. At the other end of the line are trained professionals. They listen, ask questions and look for a solution together with you. You do not have to give your name.

At 147 there are no wrong topics. Many people get in touch because of arguments in the family, trouble with friends or stress at school. Others are heartbroken, feel lonely or are being bullied. Anyone who is worried about a friend may also call. Sometimes it already helps just to tell someone everything.

The call costs nothing and does not appear on the phone bill as an expensive number. **Confidential** means that the advisers do not pass on what you tell them. Anyone who would rather write than speak can use the **chat**, a text message or an email. This way everyone can find the way that feels most comfortable for them.

147 is there for worries and questions. In an acute emergency, when someone is injured or in danger, you dial an **emergency number**: 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade, 144 for an ambulance or 112 as the European emergency number. It is good to remember these numbers, just like 147.

gewusst: Pro Juventute was founded in 1912 and has been working for children and young people in Switzerland for more than a hundred years.
The number 147 is so short so that it is easy to remember.

teile.einleitung: A child car seat protects children in the car. Because children are smaller than adults, the normal seat belt does not fit them properly, and the child seat helps with this.
wichtigste: In the car everyone always wears a seat belt.
Children need a child seat that suits their height and weight.
In Switzerland the rule applies to children under 12 who are shorter than 150 cm.
Babies travel in a baby seat that faces backwards.
The child seat must meet a valid safety standard.
In an accident the seat holds you in place with the belt.

abschnitte.titel: Why a child seat is needed
abschnitte.text: The **seat belt** in a car is made for adults. On children it would run across the neck or the tummy and could cause injuries in an accident. A **child seat** raises the child up or holds them with its own belts. This spreads the force of an impact over strong parts of the body.

In Switzerland children under **12** who are shorter than **150 centimetres** must travel in a suitable child seat. Anyone taller may use the normal belt. This rule applies on all journeys, including short ones. The parents or the person driving are responsible for it.

There are different seats depending on age. **Babies** lie in a baby seat that faces **backwards** against the direction of travel, because this protects their head and neck best. Later comes a seat with its own harness, and then a **booster seat** with a backrest. It is important that the seat suits the child’s size and is fitted correctly.

A child seat must meet a valid **safety standard**; you can see this from an orange label. The belt should fit snugly and not be twisted. If a baby seat faces backwards on the front passenger seat, the **airbag** must be switched off. Children are usually safest in the back seat.

gewusst: A crash even at town speeds is so strong that nobody could hold on to a child with their arms.
In Switzerland the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention (BFU) and motoring organisations regularly test and recommend child seats.
